| traffic light (tl) | 22 s | 7 s | 1.35 → 1.2 GB |
| red-first (rf) | 18 s | 12 s | 1.2 → 1.1 GB |
| blobs | 6 s | 6 s | 1.0 GB |

- **Native Python:** every finder now takes 3.5 to 7 seconds; before, walk took 28, tl 20, fill 16 and rf 10 seconds.
- **Memory:** about 1 GB of browser memory is Pyodide and the page itself, there before any finder runs. The finders add at most about 180 MB on top, so memory isn't a problem.

**What changed:**
- **Traffic light** now scores only the spots where the red is bright enough to become a candidate, instead of shifting the whole image 160 times.
- **Walk and fill** sample all their angles and directions in one step instead of one at a time.
- **tl, rf and fill** now share a faster exact version of the peak finder (h-maxima). It only works on the parts of the image that can matter. A new test checks it against scikit-image's version on random images.

**Proposed but not done:** all five finders are still over 5 seconds in the browser (blobs only just).
1. **Per-candidate measuring** is the next hotspot in every finder, at 1 to 2.5 seconds. Skipping candidates the finder already rejected should cut it without changing results.
2. **Reusing the image preprocessing** when you switch finders on the page would save 1 to 3 seconds per switch.
3. **Lower-precision images** (float32) would roughly halve the finders' memory. It changes results at ties, so it needs a scoring comparison first.
4. **Dropping scikit-image** would remove about 17 MB from the first page load.

The PR also adds three benchmark tools and records all results and proposals in the repo's ledger. The existing interactive and invariance tests pass, and I'm watching the PR's checks.

content.text:
From now on, algorithm and performance work runs the raw Python finders, not the web page. I've added that as a standing preference in `detection/STATE.md` and in project memory, and pushed it to PR #257.

`bench.py` now times each finder the same way `nor_lab.py` runs it. The two browser benchmarks stay only as a check that the page itself still works. Here are the raw Python times after the speed-ups:

| finder | time | passes / candidates |
|---|---|---|
| traffic light (tl) | 3.9 s | 229 / 463 |
| blobs | 2.8 s | 244 / 1649 |
| walk | 5.1 s | 249 / 1382 |
| fill | 5.3 s | 213 / 909 |
| red-first (rf) | 6.6 s | 265 / 1263 |

Peak memory is 180 to 380 MB per finder. Walk, fill and red-first are still slightly over 5 seconds. For all three, the next thing to speed up is the per-candidate measuring step (`nor3.finish`), which the ledger lists as the first proposal.

entries.description: Get information on a specific pull request in GitHub repository.

after.description: Cursor for pagination, used only by the get_review_comments method. Pass the endCursor from the previous page's PageInfo to fetch the next page.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.

name: nor-web-page
description: NoR Finder browser page (web/, R8, PR #225) - Ariel's requirements, Pyodide design, GitHub Pages via github-pages pack
metadata:
  type: project
  modified: 2026-09-28T17:26:56.305Z
---

Ariel (2026-09-28) asked for a no-backend web page, served from GitHub Pages. It opens an image, detects once, then shows every filter and its parameters as live dials, with a cropped list of passing NoRs and their measurements, and a summary. The requirements are R8 in docs/requirements.md.

Ariel's rules for the page:
- The blue mask is only a filter (N), in every finder.
- Detection settings are dials too, with a note that they take time.
- All finders are offered, traffic light by default.
- Filter settings persist in localStorage, with "Restore filter defaults".
- Third-party files are cached for 30 days (service worker + Cache Storage, since localStorage is too small).
- A ★ keeper stays in the list whatever the filters say.

**Design:** detection/interactive.py (Session.detect / refilter) runs under Pyodide in web/worker.js. Python modules are imported straight from the published detection/ and src/, so there is no build list. tifffile is vendored by web/build.py.

**Deploy:** the canon github-pages pack was adopted in PR #225. Issue #226 holds the two Pages settings only Ariel can set. After merge, force the first release: `gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=github-pages/site-release`.

**Testing:** headless Chromium needs `--ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<proxy CA SPKI>` to trust the session proxy's CA. See [[repo-is-home]].

**Layout (Ariel 2026-09-28, PR #228):**
- The header holds the logo, title and theme switch.
- The left bar holds the image box (R/G/B layer checkboxes), the finder box (MAIN settings, Advanced, and a Find Candidates button that shines when stale; nothing auto-runs on load) and the filters.
- The main area switches between the image view and the items view.
- The right bar holds the summary. A status bar sits at the bottom.
- Logo: the three Sagol School marks traced to SVG in red, green and blue (web/logo_trace.py regenerates it).
- Frame (Ariel 2026-09-28, PR #230): static frame (header 52px, footer 1cm) and only the columns scroll. The footer shows the site version, stamped by the public-website pack (package.json is the record).
- Help (Ariel 2026-09-28, PR #232): detection/finder_help.py holds ABOUT per finder and HELP per setting; a test fails if a shown setting lacks help. Site version major is 0 (0.10928.x); the release bumps the build.
- Round 3 (Ariel 2026-09-29, PR #235): drag/wheel-zoom/sideways-step; selection card in right bar (decisions live on cards, not image clicks); Finalists/Rejected views with crop Options and length adjusters; Downloads box; ground truth = JSON (norfinder-ground-truth/1) read by `nor_lab.py --labels` (read_labels, measure_error), chosen over a mask; page-only filter letters/titles in finder_help.REASONS (lab REASONS letters unchanged); Session.alone gives per-filter independent counts. Google Drive loading: public links via Drive API v3 + API key (PR #242). Ariel 2026-09-29: key lives in repo VARIABLE GOOGLE_API_KEY (not config file; secrets cannot reach Pages), declared in .github/site.config build_vars and written into web/config.js by web/build.py (PR #247); release fails until the variable is set. Steps in issue #234 (done; live 0.10929.4 works). DRIVE_DEFAULT_FOLDER repo variable = link the Drive dialog opens on first (PR #250).

def hmax_above(img, h, T):
    """skimage h_maxima(img, h) & (img > T), bit for bit, but reconstructing only the pieces of
    img that rise above T - h. Pixels below that level cannot carry a reconstruction value up to
    a pixel above T (flat reconstruction commutes with max(., L)), so each piece is independent."""
    from skimage.morphology import h_maxima
    from skimage.morphology.grayreconstruct import reconstruction
    if h > np.ptp(img):
        return np.zeros(img.shape, bool)
    L = T - h - 1e-6 * max(1.0, float(np.abs(img).max()))
    if (img > L).mean() > 0.5:      # most of the image: nothing to save
        return h_maxima(img, h).astype(bool) & (img > T)
    shifted = img - h - 2 * np.finfo(img.dtype).resolution * np.abs(img)   # as h_maxima does
    lab, _ = ndi.label(img > L, EIGHT); out = np.zeros(img.shape, bool)
    for i, sl in enumerate(ndi.find_objects(lab)):
        inside = lab[sl] == i + 1; top = inside & (img[sl] > T)
        if not top.any():
            continue
        ms = np.where(inside, img[sl], L)
        rec = reconstruction(np.where(inside, shifted[sl], L), ms, method='dilation')
        out[sl] |= top & (ms - rec >= h)
    return out


def classify(caspr, nav, bm, p):
    valid = ~bm
    cn = ndi.gaussian_filter(nor.norm(caspr, valid), p['smooth'])

    """Geometry along the stick axis, which runs from one green's centroid to the other's.
    length: extent of green+red+green along the axis; width: its area / length (mean width,
    so a ragged pixel on the edge does not count as the width)."""
    g1, g2, r = c['greens'][0], c['greens'][1], c['red']
    a1, a2 = g1.sum(), g2.sum()

    p1 = np.array(np.nonzero(g1)).mean(1); p2 = np.array(np.nonzero(g2)).mean(1)
    ax = p2 - p1; ax = ax / max(np.hypot(*ax), 1e-9)          # (dy, dx)
    union = g1 | g2 | r
    ys, xs = np.nonzero(union); t = ys * ax[0] + xs * ax[1]
    length = float(t.max() - t.min() + 1)
    ry, rx = np.nonzero(r); tr_ = ry * ax[0] + rx * ax[1]
    c['length_px'] = length
    c['red_len_px'] = float(tr_.max() - tr_.min() + 1)
    c['width_px'] = float(union.sum() / length)
    c['aspect'] = length / c['width_px']
    c['axis'] = ax
    # the measuring lines, in box pixel coordinates (y, x): the length line runs along the axis
    # through the stick's middle; the width line crosses it at the red's centre
    nv = np.array([ax[1], -ax[0]])

    pt = lambda t, s_: (t * ax[0] + s_ * nv[0], t * ax[1] + s_ * nv[1])
    t0, t1 = t.min() - 0.5, t.max() + 0.5

def hmax_above(img, h, T):
    """skimage h_maxima(img, h) & (img > T), bit for bit, but reconstructing only the pieces of
    img that rise above T - h. Pixels below that level cannot carry a reconstruction value up to
    a pixel above T (flat reconstruction commutes with max(., L)), so each piece is independent."""
    from skimage.morphology import h_maxima
    from skimage.morphology.grayreconstruct import reconstruction
    if h > np.ptp(img):
        return np.zeros(img.shape, bool)
    L = T - h - 1e-6 * max(1.0, float(img.max()), -float(img.min()))
    if (img > L).mean() > 0.5:      # most of the image: nothing to save
        return h_maxima(img, h).astype(bool) & (img > T)
    lab, n = ndi.label(img > L, EIGHT); out = np.zeros(img.shape, bool)
    if n == 0:
        return out
    sls = ndi.find_objects(lab); keep = np.unique(lab[img > T])      # the pieces reaching above T
    # pieces are independent, so several can share one reconstruction call (the others held at L):
    # group them by the tile their box starts in, which saves the per-call cost of tiny pieces
    groups = {}
    for i in keep:
        sl = sls[i - 1]; groups.setdefault((sl[0].start // 128, sl[1].start // 128), []).append(i)
    for ids in groups.values():
        y0 = min(sls[i - 1][0].start for i in ids); y1 = max(sls[i - 1][0].stop for i in ids)
        x0 = min(sls[i - 1][1].start for i in ids); x1 = max(sls[i - 1][1].stop for i in ids)
        sl = (slice(y0, y1), slice(x0, x1))
        inside = np.isin(lab[sl], ids); top = inside & (img[sl] > T)
        ms = np.where(inside, img[sl], L)
        shifted = img[sl] - h - 2 * np.finfo(img.dtype).resolution * np.abs(img[sl])   # as h_maxima does
        rec = reconstruction(np.where(inside, shifted, L), ms, method='dilation')
        out[sl] |= top & (ms - rec >= h)
    return out

_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jh?thread=cmsg_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jhHhad61xSXRDj9d4c7RuyQf)_

Before: running the raw Python finders on the reference slide took walk 21.6 s, tl 15.0 s, fill 11.7 s, rf 9.6 s and blobs 2.7 s. There was no tool to measure the finders' time or memory.

After: tl takes 3.2 s, walk 4.5 s, fill 4.8 s, rf 5.7 s and blobs 2.4 s, with every candidate, verdict and measurement bit-identical to main (`perf.py check`, whose signature now covers every measurement). On the live page, detection drops from 22 to 7 s for tl and from 43 to 12 s for walk.

How:
- **tl** scores only the pixels whose red window can reach `s_min`, because no other pixel can become a peak. It samples them with `map_coordinates` instead of making 160 whole-image `ndi.shift`s.
- **walk and fill** make one `_bilinear` call covering every strip offset, angle and bend.
- **`nor3.hmax_above`** (used by tl, rf and fill) reconstructs h-maxima only over the parts of the image above T − h. The pieces are batched by tile. The result is exact because flat reconstruction commutes with max(·, L).
- **`finish`** dilates the red rim once and uses a single square dilation, and `nor3.median` skips `np.median`'s per-call overhead. **`FibreAngle`** smooths the structure tensor only on the rows a finder reads.
- **Tools:** `detection/bench.py` measures the raw finders' time and memory, which is where algorithm work is measured (Ariel's rule, now in STATE.md). `browser/bench_pyodide.mjs` and `browser/bench_live.mjs` measure the page runtime only.
- The ledger (`lab/ledger.md` §4) has every attempt, including one dropped, and the remaining proposals.

Tests: `tests/test_speedups.py` fuzzes each helper against the call it replaces. It passes, as do `tests/test_interactive.py` and `tests/test_invariance.py`.

I've pushed a second round of speed-ups to PR #257. Every finder still gives exactly the same result as main: every candidate, verdict and measurement matches bit for bit.

Raw Python times on the reference slide, main's code against now:

| finder | main | now |
|---|---|---|
| traffic light (tl) | 15.0 s | 3.2 s |
| walk | 21.6 s | 4.5 s |
| fill | 11.7 s | 4.8 s |
| red-first (rf) | 9.6 s | 5.7 s |
| blobs | 2.7 s | 2.4 s |

To prove nothing changed, I extended `perf.py check` so it compares every measurement, not just the positions and verdicts. It reports identical output on all six finder variants. Each new helper also has a test in `tests/test_speedups.py` that compares it against the call it replaces, and the existing interactive test passes.

- **Red-first is the only finder still over 5 seconds.** What's left there is spread across many small per-candidate steps, with no single hotspot.
- **I dropped the float32 idea.** It changes results at ties, and you've ruled out any quality loss for speed.

The ledger in the PR records every attempt, including one I dropped because it was slower and not exact.

I asked the project's coordinator to open a separate thread for the Pyodide memory breakdown and options; it isn't open yet.
